title: New technologies help Natural History Museum uncover 92 species in its transformed gardens
excerpt: The Natural History Museum's transformed gardens in South Kensington are revealing new insights into London's urban wildlife. content_html:
The Natural History Museum's transformed gardens in South Kensington are revealing new insights into London's urban wildlife. Among the 92 species recorded at the site for the first time between its reopening in July 2024 and the end of 2025 are the striking emperor moth and small red-eyed damselfly.

The discoveries build on the gardens' rich biodiversity and mark a new chapter for the museum's 5-acre (2-hectare) outdoor site, now transformed into a network of interconnected habitats, from chalk grasslands to woodlands, designed to support wildlife, engage visitors and advance scientific understanding of urban ecosystems.

Alongside traditional species surveys and visual observations, museum scientists are using pioneering techniques including environmental DNA (eDNA), acoustic monitoring and a growing network of environmental sensors. Together, these approaches are generating millions of records and opening up new ways to investigate how wildlife responds to changes in habitat, climate and human activity. The research is described in an article in The London Naturalist.

The gardens have a long history of biological recording, with 3,500 species documented since monitoring began in 1995. These include several arthropod species recorded for the first time in the U.K., as well as numerous first regional records.

The Nature Discovery Garden now provides an opportunity to investigate biodiversity across a much larger and more varied area, from woodland and meadow habitats to ponds, planted areas and spaces designed to demonstrate climate-resilient gardening. The latest discoveries add to this extensive record and highlight the potential of urban green spaces to support biodiversity. Among the latest additions are:

  • Emperor moth (Saturnia pavonia)—one of Britain's most striking moths, with distinctive eye-like markings on its wings.
  • Red beard-moss (Bryoerythrophyllum recurvirostrum)—a moss with slender green leaves and characteristic reddish-brown coloring—was recorded for the first time in the gardens at the base of a large London plane tree.
  • Asian mud-dauber wasp (Sceliphron curvatum)—a solitary wasp originating from Asia. Females construct distinctive mud nests containing paralyzed spiders, which provide food for their developing larvae.
  • Cotton seed bug (Oxycarenus hyalinipennis)—the first known British specimen of the bug was found by sweeping short vegetation on the garden's chalk hillside.
  • Peregrine falcon (Falco peregrinus)—Since March 2024, 24 species have been recorded, including four not previously recorded, among them this large bird of prey.

Ed Baker, acoustic biology researcher at the Natural History Museum, said, "Recording 92 new species in our new gardens shows just how much wildlife can thrive in the heart of London. By combining traditional wildlife surveys with new technologies, we can better understand how urban nature responds to changes in climate, habitat and human activity—and how we can make our cities better places for both people and wildlife."

A major development since the gardens reopened has been the introduction of new scientific technologies that allow researchers to monitor the environment in unprecedented detail. In 2025, the museum switched on a network of environmental sensors across its Nature Discovery Garden. In 2026, the network grew to more than 50 sensors and generated over 11 million environmental data records in its first year. The technology is enabling scientists to investigate aspects of urban nature that would be difficult to capture through conventional ecological surveys alone.

All these data streams are being brought together through the museum's developing Data Ecosystem, built using AWS cloud technologies in partnership with Amazon Web Services (AWS). The museum is currently extending its sensor network into the Evolution Garden to allow scientists to compare habitats with different planting styles and levels of visitor activity, helping to understand how people and nature interact in urban green spaces.

The new monitoring technology is already helping scientists investigate one of the major environmental challenges facing cities: rising temperatures. During the June 2026 heat wave, soil temperature sensors in the museum's woodland areas recorded temperatures 10°C cooler than those in the paved areas of the Darwin Center Courtyard.

The museum's gardens are also providing an opportunity to investigate how conservation interventions affect entire ecological communities. One ongoing project is examining the consequences of transferring pond material from the former Wildlife Garden into the new Nature Discovery Garden. Researchers are investigating how this intervention influences biodiversity and the development of the new pond ecosystem.

The research is not confined to scientists working behind the scenes. Visitors, schools, volunteers and community groups can all contribute to understanding urban nature through wildlife recording, field surveys and community science initiatives.
